questions.q: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix and $|A| = 5$, then $|2A|$ is:
questions.solution:
For an $n \times n$ matrix, $|kA| = k^{n}|A|$ — the scalar multiplies **every** one of the $n$ rows.

Here $n = 3$ and $k = 2$:

$|2A| = 2^{3} \times 5 = 8 \times 5 = \mathbf{40}$.

Answering $10$ is the common error, from treating it like $|kA| = k|A|$.

questions.q: For matrices $A$ and $B$ of compatible order, $(AB)^{T}$ equals:
questions.solution:
$(AB)^{T} = \mathbf{B^{T}A^{T}}$ — the **order reverses**.

It has to: if $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, then $A^{T}B^{T}$ would be $n\times m$ times $p\times n$, which is not even defined unless $m = p$.

The same reversal applies to inverses: $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$.

questions.q: A square matrix $A$ has an inverse if and only if:
questions.solution:
$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}(A)$, which requires division by $|A|$ — so the inverse exists exactly when $\mathbf{|A| \neq 0}$.

Such a matrix is called **non-singular** or invertible. A matrix with $|A| = 0$ is singular and has no inverse.

questions.q: If two rows of a determinant are identical, its value is:
questions.solution:
Swapping two rows changes the sign of a determinant. If the two rows are **identical**, swapping them leaves the matrix unchanged, so

$|A| = -|A| \Rightarrow 2|A| = 0 \Rightarrow |A| = \mathbf{0}$.

The same holds for two identical columns, or more generally whenever one row is a linear combination of the others — the rows are then linearly dependent.

Matrix multiplication is **associative**, $(AB)C = A(BC)$, and distributive over addition — but **not commutative**: in general $AB \neq BA$.

Often $BA$ is not even defined when $AB$ is. Even for square matrices the two usually differ, which is a genuine departure from ordinary arithmetic and the source of many errors.

If $|A| \neq 0$ then $A^{-1}$ exists, and

$X = A^{-1}B$

is the one and only solution. So the system is **consistent with a unique solution**.

When $|A| = 0$ the system is either inconsistent (no solution) or has infinitely many, depending on whether $(\text{adj}A)B$ is zero — which is what Cramer's rule distinguishes.

Skew-symmetric means $\mathbf{A^{T} = -A}$.

A consequence worth knowing: every **diagonal element must be zero**, since $a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$ forces $a_{ii} = 0$.

Also, the determinant of any skew-symmetric matrix of **odd** order is zero, because $|A| = |A^{T}| = |-A| = (-1)^{n}|A|$, and for odd $n$ that gives $|A| = -|A|$.

questions.q: For square matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same order, $|AB|$ equals:
questions.solution:
$|AB| = \mathbf{|A||B|}$ — the determinant is multiplicative.

Notice that although $AB \neq BA$ in general, their determinants are always equal, since $|A||B| = |B||A|$.

It follows at once that $|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}$, by taking $B = A^{-1}$.

questions.q: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix, then $|\text{adj}(A)|$ equals:
questions.solution:
In general $|\text{adj}(A)| = |A|^{n-1}$ for an $n \times n$ matrix.

For $n = 3$: $|\text{adj}(A)| = \mathbf{|A|^{2}}$.

It follows from $A\cdot\text{adj}(A) = |A|I$: taking determinants gives $|A||\text{adj}A| = |A|^{n}$.

questions.q: If $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix with $|A| = 3$, find $|3A|$.
If $|A| = 4$ for a $3\times3$ matrix, find $|A^{-1}|$. Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution:
$AA^{-1} = I$, so taking determinants:

$|A||A^{-1}| = |I| = 1$

$|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|} = \dfrac{1}{4} = \mathbf{0.25}$.

The order of the matrix does not enter into it.

questions.q: A matrix $A$ is of order $2\times3$ and $B$ is of order $3\times4$. How many columns does $AB$ have?
questions.solution:
For $AB$ to be defined, the inner dimensions must match — and $3 = 3$, so it is.

The product takes the **outer** dimensions: $AB$ is $2 \times 4$.

So it has $\mathbf{4}$ columns. (Note $BA$ is not defined here, since $4 \neq 2$.)

questions.q: What is the value of every diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix?
questions.solution:
Skew-symmetry means $a_{ij} = -a_{ji}$ for all $i, j$.

Put $i = j$:

$a_{ii} = -a_{ii} \Rightarrow 2a_{ii} = 0 \Rightarrow a_{ii} = \mathbf{0}$.

Every diagonal entry must be zero.

questions.q: Explain how a system of three linear equations in three unknowns is solved by the matrix method $X = A^{-1}B$. State the condition for a unique solution, and describe what happens when $|A| = 0$, distinguishing the inconsistent case from the case of infinitely many solutions. Give the geometric meaning of each.
questions.solution:
**Setting up.** Three linear equations in $x$, $y$, $z$:

$a_1x + b_1y + c_1z = d_1$

$a_2x + b_2y + c_2z = d_2$

$a_3x + b_3y + c_3z = d_3$

are written as the single matrix equation $AX = B$, where

$A = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{pmatrix}$, $X = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \\ d_3 \end{pmatrix}$

**The method.** If $A^{-1}$ exists, premultiply both sides by it:

$A^{-1}(AX) = A^{-1}B$

$(A^{-1}A)X = A^{-1}B$

$IX = A^{-1}B$

$\boxed{X = A^{-1}B}$

In practice $A^{-1}$ is found as $\dfrac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}(A)$.

**Case 1: $|A| \neq 0$ — a unique solution.**

The system is **consistent** and $X = A^{-1}B$ gives the one and only answer.

**Geometrically**, each equation is a **plane** in three-dimensional space. A non-zero determinant means the three normal vectors are linearly independent, so the planes are genuinely tilted with respect to one another and meet at exactly **one point** — whose coordinates are the solution.

**Case 2: $|A| = 0$.** $A^{-1}$ does not exist, so the method above fails and the system is **singular**. There are two sub-cases, told apart by computing $(\text{adj}A)B$.

**2a: $(\text{adj}A)B \neq 0$ — inconsistent, no solution.**

**Geometrically**, the planes have no point in common. This happens when two planes are parallel and distinct, or when the three planes form a **triangular prism**: each pair meets in a line, but the three lines are parallel and never share a point. The prism case is the one people forget, because no two planes are parallel and yet there is still no solution.

**2b: $(\text{adj}A)B = 0$ — consistent, with infinitely many solutions.**

**Geometrically**, the planes share more than a single point. Either all three planes **meet in a common line**, giving a one-parameter family of solutions, or the three equations describe the **same plane**, giving a two-parameter family.

**The homogeneous case.** When $B = 0$ the system $AX = 0$ always has the **trivial solution** $x = y = z = 0$, so it can never be inconsistent — every plane passes through the origin, so they always share at least that point.

$|A| \neq 0$: only the trivial solution — the three planes meet at the origin alone.

$|A| = 0$: infinitely many **non-trivial** solutions — the planes share a common line or plane through the origin.

This is why $|A| = 0$ is exactly the condition for a homogeneous system to have a non-trivial solution, a fact used constantly in eigenvalue problems.

**Summary.** The determinant answers the question of **how many** solutions there are; when it vanishes, $(\text{adj}A)B$ answers whether that number is zero or infinite. No case gives two or three solutions, because the solution set of a linear system is always a point, a line, a plane, or empty.
